title: Deuteronomy 2:26–37
context: Moses sends Sihon king of Heshbon an offer of peace, asking only to pass through on the highway and pay for food and water. Sihon refuses, because the LORD hardened his spirit to deliver him into Israel’s hand. Sihon attacks at Jahaz, and Israel defeats him, devotes his cities to destruction, takes the livestock, and occupies the land from the Arnon to Gilead, avoiding Ammon as God commanded.

verses.text: I sent messengers out of the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon king of Heshbon with words of peace, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Moses sends words of peace to Sihon. Even with the land already promised, Israel first offers peaceful passage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same offer. Both traditions see this as consistent with the law’s later instruction to offer peace before battle (Deuteronomy 20:10).

verses.text: “Let me pass through your land. I will go along by the highway. I will turn neither to the right hand nor to the left.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel promises to keep to the highway and not turn aside. The request is modest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read it the same way. This is shared ground.

verses.text: You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat; and give me water for money, that I may drink. Just let me pass through on my feet,
verses.arminianNotes: Israel will pay for food and water and only pass through. The request mirrors the treatment of Edom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. This is shared ground.

verses.text: as the children of Esau who dwell in Seir, and the Moabites who dwell in Ar, did to me, until I pass over the Jordan into the land which the LORD our God gives us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses points to Edom and Moab as examples, and to Israel’s goal across the Jordan. Numbers 20:14–21 says Edom refused passage; interpreters often reconcile the two by suggesting that, although Edom refused passage through its land, Edomites along the border still sold food and water to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same tension and similar harmonizations. This is shared ground.

verses.text: But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into your hand, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes: Sihon refuses because “the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate.” Arminian readers typically read this as judicial hardening: God confirms and gives over a king already set against him, in line with the judgment on Amorite sin anticipated in Genesis 15:16. Sihon remains responsible for his refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers typically read the verse as God’s sovereign purpose working through Sihon’s willing sin: God ordained the refusal to bring about Israel’s victory, while Sihon acted freely and is justly accountable. They see the same pattern in Pharaoh (Exodus 9:12; Romans 9:18).
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm that God hardened Sihon, that Sihon was guilty, and that God used his refusal to give Israel the land. Classical Arminians typically read the hardening as God’s judicial response to Sihon’s own prior hostility. Reformed interpreters typically read it as God’s decree working through Sihon’s free choice, so that divine purpose and human responsibility are both fully real.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Behold, I have begun to deliver up Sihon and his land before you. Begin to possess, that you may inherit his land.”
verses.arminianNotes: God says he has begun to deliver Sihon and his land to Israel. Israel must begin to possess it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same pairing of gift and action. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Sihon comes out to fight at Jahaz with all his people. He chooses war after peace was offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that Sihon’s attack is his own act. This is shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD our God delivered him up before us; and we struck him, his sons, and all his people.
verses.arminianNotes: God delivered him up, and Israel struck him, his sons, and his people. The victory is credited to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read it the same way. This is shared ground.

verses.text: We took all his cities at that time, and utterly destroyed every inhabited city, with the women and the little ones. We left no one remaining.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel devotes every inhabited city to destruction, including women and children. This practice, often called herem, is one of Scripture’s hardest moral questions. Many Arminian interpreters treat it as a unique, limited act of divine judgment on long-standing sin, not a pattern for other wars or for the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters likewise treat it as God’s judgment through Israel at a particular point in redemptive history, not a model for later believers. Both traditions acknowledge the difficulty and differ internally on how to explain it; neither treats it as permission for violence today.

verses.text: Only the livestock we took for plunder for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities which we had taken.
verses.arminianNotes: Only the livestock and plunder are kept. The note shows that this herem allowed spoil, unlike some later cases (Joshua 6:17–19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read it the same way. This is shared ground.

verses.text: From Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the valley, even to Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God delivered up all before us.
verses.arminianNotes: From Aroer to Gilead, no city was too strong, because “the LORD our God delivered up all before us.” The fear of fortified cities (1:28) is answered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same contrast with the earlier fear. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Only to the land of the children of Ammon you didn’t come near: all the banks of the river Jabbok, and the cities of the hill country, and wherever the LORD our God forbade us.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel did not approach Ammon’s land, obeying God’s limits. Victory did not mean taking whatever they could.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that obedience includes respecting God’s boundaries. This is shared ground.
